---
title: "NHANES"
description: "National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey: US population health survey with interviews, exams, and lab tests. Open access."
---

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) is run by the
CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). It combines interviews,
physical examinations, and laboratory tests on a sample designed to represent
the US civilian noninstitutionalized population. It has run continuously since
1999, and data are released in two-year cycles.

- **Website and data:** [wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/default.aspx)
- **Tutorials:** [NHANES tutorials](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/default.aspx)
- **Access:** open. Public-use files need no application.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Ask Tomás before you download
The lab collaborates on easier ways to access and download NHANES data. Ask
Tomás about them before you write your own download scripts.
:::

## How the data are organized

- Each cycle is split into components (demographics, dietary, examination,
  laboratory, questionnaire), and each component into many data files.
- Public files are SAS transport (`.xpt`) files. Read them with
  `pandas.read_sas(path, format="xport")` in Python or `haven::read_xpt()` in
  R.
- Merge files within a cycle on `SEQN`, the respondent sequence number. Some
  files have more than one row per participant, so check before you merge.
- Fieldwork stopped in March 2020 because of COVID-19. The 2019–March 2020
  data were combined with 2017–2018 into the 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic
  files; use those rather than 2019–2020 on its own. The next cycle is August
  2021–August 2023.

## Use the survey design

NHANES isn't a simple random sample: some groups are oversampled, and
participants are selected in stages. Unweighted estimates don't represent the
US population, and ignoring the design makes standard errors too small. NCHS
recommends using the sample weights and design variables in all analyses. The
[tutorials](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/default.aspx) explain
this in detail; read them before your first analysis.

- **Weights** are in the demographics file: `WTINT2YR` for interview data,
  `WTMEC2YR` for anything measured at the mobile examination center (MEC).
  Some lab tests are run on subsamples with their own weights. Use the weight
  for the smallest subsample your variables come from.
- **Design variables:** `SDMVSTRA` (pseudo-stratum) and `SDMVPSU`
  (pseudo-PSU).
- **Pooling cycles:** NCHS recommends combining cycles into four years or more
  when possible. Divide the two-year weights by the number of cycles you pool;
  for two cycles, `WTMEC4YR = WTMEC2YR / 2`. The tutorials cover the
  exceptions.
- **Subgroups:** define the design on the full sample, then subset the design
  object. Dropping rows first gives wrong standard errors.

In R, with the `survey` package:

```r
library(survey)

des <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU, strata = ~SDMVSTRA, weights = ~WTMEC2YR,
  nest = TRUE, data = nhanes
)
adults <- subset(des, RIDAGEYR >= 20)
svymean(~BMXBMI, adults, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Beyond the public files

- **Restricted-use data**, such as detailed geography, are only available
  through the NCHS [Research Data Center](https://www.cdc.gov/rdc/).
- **Mortality follow-up:** NCHS publishes
  [linked mortality files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/linked-data/mortality-files/)
  for NHANES participants. The public-use versions alter some values to
  protect participants' identities.
